questions.question: What is sync.Mutex, and how do Lock and Unlock protect shared state?
questions.title: sync.Mutex fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: A sync.Mutex is a mutual-exclusion lock that allows only one holder into a protected critical section at a time. Its zero value is unlocked and ready to use. Lock waits until ownership can be acquired, and Unlock releases it. Every access participating in the shared invariant must follow the same locking rule, and the Mutex must not be copied after first use.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands exclusion, the zero value, consistent protection, and the no-copy rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The zero value of sync.Mutex is an unlocked, usable lock.
Lock blocks until the caller acquires the critical section.
Unlock releases the lock; unlocking an unlocked Mutex panics.
Protect every conflicting read and write with the same rule.
A Mutex must not be copied after its first use.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`sync.Mutex` provides mutual exclusion around shared mutable state. When one goroutine holds the lock, another call to `Lock` waits. The zero value is already an unlocked mutex, so embedding one directly in a struct is the normal pattern.

A critical section begins after `Lock` returns and ends at `Unlock`. The protected data and its lock should live close together, usually as unexported fields with pointer-receiver methods. That makes it difficult for callers to access the data without following the lock contract.

For example, a `Counter` can store an integer beside a Mutex. `Inc` locks, changes the value, and unlocks. `Value` also locks before reading. Locking only the write would leave a conflicting ordinary read unsynchronized, so both methods use the same guard.

The lock protects state; it does not automatically make a copied object safe. A Mutex must not be copied after first use because the copy has different lock state guarding data that may still be shared. Pointer receivers and returning a pointer to the containing object help preserve one identity.

I keep critical sections small, avoid blocking network or channel work while holding the lock, and ensure every successful Lock has one Unlock. A defer immediately after Lock is useful when a function has several return paths. The goal is not to lock everything; it is to give one explicit synchronization rule to one shared invariant.

sections.title: Put the guard beside the guarded value
sections.content: A lock is understandable only when readers can identify what it protects. Encapsulating the Mutex and state in one type turns an informal convention into a small API: callers request operations, and those methods enforce the critical section.

sections.title: Concept guide · sync.Mutex fundamentals
sections.content:
An increment is a read-modify-write sequence, not one indivisible ordinary memory action. Without synchronization, two goroutines can read the same old value and both write the same result. Placing that sequence between Lock and Unlock permits only one goroutine to perform it at a time.

Mutual exclusion also establishes ordering. In the Go memory model, an Unlock is synchronized before a later Lock on the same Mutex returns. A goroutine that acquires the lock can therefore observe writes completed by the previous holder. A sleep or scheduler yield creates no comparable guarantee.

Reads belong to the contract too. If one goroutine writes a field under a Mutex while another reads it without that Mutex or an appropriate atomic operation, the program can still contain a data race. Expose read methods such as Value or Snapshot that acquire the same guard.

The zero value avoids constructor ceremony, but the value has identity after use. Copying a struct containing a used Mutex duplicates the synchronization word, not the shared history. Keep methods on pointer receivers, avoid returning the struct by value, and heed `go vet` copylocks warnings. Do not rely on copying before a particular call being harmless unless the whole object's ownership is unambiguous.

Unlocking an unlocked Mutex panics. Go Mutex is also not reentrant: a goroutine that locks the same Mutex again before unlocking it will block itself. Keep helper boundaries clear about whether the caller already holds the lock, and prefer small public methods that acquire it exactly once.

sections.title: One critical section at a time
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant G1 as Goroutine A
  participant M as Mutex + state
  participant G2 as Goroutine B
  G1->>M: Lock succeeds
  G2->>M: Lock waits
  G1->>M: Read, modify, write
  G1->>M: Unlock
  M-->>G2: Lock now succeeds
  G2->>M: Read current state
```

questions.question: How should you choose the scope of a Mutex critical section?
questions.title: Choosing a safe Mutex critical section
questions.direct_answer: A critical section should include every read and write needed to preserve one shared invariant, but exclude unrelated slow work. Lock before checking the protected state, make the complete state transition while holding the lock, and unlock afterward. Splitting a check from its update can create a logical race even if each individual access is locked; holding a lock during I/O can create avoidable contention.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can protect a multi-field invariant without making the critical section unnecessarily broad.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Define the invariant before deciding where to lock.
Keep a dependent check and update in one critical section.
Use one guard consistently for every field in that invariant.
Copy required input before slow I/O; do not hold the lock unnecessarily.
Measure contention before introducing more complicated locking.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Mutex scope comes from the state rule the code must preserve. A critical section needs to cover the complete operation that observes and changes that rule, not merely the line that performs the final assignment.

Suppose a ledger requires the total of two account balances to remain constant during a transfer. Checking the source balance under one lock call and changing balances under another leaves a gap in which another transfer can invalidate the decision. The check and both updates belong under the same guard.

At the same time, a large critical section reduces concurrency. Database calls, network requests, channel sends, logging hooks, and expensive calculations can block while every other goroutine waits. I prepare independent work first, lock only for the shared state transition, copy any value needed later, then unlock before slow external work.

For example, a Ledger can keep one Mutex beside its accounts map. `Transfer` locks once, validates both accounts and funds, applies both balance changes, and returns. `Balance` uses the same lock for its read. A single lock is easier to reason about than separate account locks for this beginner-sized invariant.

I start with the simplest correct lock boundary and use profiling or contention measurements before splitting locks or switching to RWMutex. Correctness is the fixed requirement; lock granularity is an optimization. The best scope makes the protected invariant obvious while allowing unrelated work to proceed independently.

sections.title: Protect the rule, not just a variable
sections.content: Several fields can form one invariant. The meaningful unit of exclusion is the state transition that must appear indivisible to other goroutines. A small lock around only one field can be too narrow; a lock around network work can be too broad.

sections.title: Find the linearization point
sections.content:
Begin by writing the invariant in plain language. For a transfer, balances must never be debited without the matching credit, and a source must not spend funds already consumed by another accepted transfer. Those conditions identify which values and decisions need one serialized operation.

Lock before reading the protected balance. Validate existence and available funds while still holding the lock. Apply debit and credit before unlocking. To another goroutine using the same guard, the transfer appears to happen at one point between Lock and Unlock; it cannot observe the half-completed state.

Now inspect everything else in the function. Parsing an already-owned argument needs no lock. Calling a remote fraud service while locked makes local balance readers depend on network latency. Sending to an unbuffered channel may wait for a receiver and can form a lock-cycle deadlock. Move independent slow operations outside, or redesign the workflow if their result must participate atomically.

Multiple locks make ordering part of the contract. If one operation locks account A then B while another locks B then A, they can deadlock. A single ledger lock avoids that class of bug at the cost of less parallelism. Sharding or ordered multi-lock acquisition should follow demonstrated contention, not anticipation.

Tests should run many transfers concurrently, then inspect the invariant under the guard after all workers finish. Run those tests with `-race`, but remember that a race-free result does not prove the business invariant: a check-then-act operation can be fully locked at each access and still be logically wrong if the combined transition is split.

sections.title: A complete protected transition
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Prepare independent input] --> B[Lock ledger]
  B --> C[Read source and destination]
  C --> D{Funds available?}
  D -- No --> E[Unlock and return error]
  D -- Yes --> F[Debit and credit together]
  F --> G[Copy result]
  G --> H[Unlock]
  H --> I[Logging or external I/O]
```

questions.question: What common mistakes cause Mutex races or deadlocks in Go?
questions.title: Common sync.Mutex mistakes
questions.direct_answer: Common Mutex mistakes are copying a used lock, forgetting an Unlock on an early return, locking only writers while readers remain unprotected, locking the same non-reentrant Mutex twice, and acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order. Keep the lock beside its data, use pointer receivers, cover all exit paths, define one access rule, and avoid holding a lock during blocking operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner recognizes copy, balance, reentrancy, access-policy, and lock-order failures.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Do not copy a Mutex or a struct containing one after use.
Every successful Lock needs exactly one reachable Unlock.
A Mutex is not reentrant; locking it twice can self-deadlock.
Unprotected readers can race with protected writers.
Acquire multiple locks in one documented global order.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The first Mutex mistake is losing the lock's identity. Passing a used lock or a struct containing it by value creates a copy with separate internal state. Code may then believe it shares one guard while different goroutines actually lock different copies. Pointer receivers and `go vet` help prevent this.

The second group is unbalanced ownership. A return or panic path that skips Unlock can leave every later caller blocked. Deferring Unlock immediately after a successful Lock is a clear choice for short functions with several exits. Conversely, an extra Unlock on an unlocked Mutex panics.

A third mistake is an incomplete access policy. Protecting every write but reading the same field directly elsewhere still permits a data race. All conflicting accesses need the same Mutex, a suitable atomic operation, or a design in which one goroutine owns the value.

Deadlocks appear when code locks a non-reentrant Mutex twice, holds a lock while waiting for work that needs the same lock, or acquires multiple locks in opposite orders. For example, transfer code that locks source then destination needs a stable ordering rule across every caller.

I make the containing type own unexported state, expose pointer-receiver operations, return snapshots rather than the live map, and keep blocking work outside the critical section. A Mutex is simple when its invariant, identity, and acquisition order are visible; most failures come from breaking one of those three boundaries.

sections.title: Five failures, three underlying boundaries
sections.content: Copying breaks lock identity. Missing or recursive operations break acquisition balance. Partial protection and inconsistent order break the shared protocol. Reviewing those boundaries is more reliable than scattering additional Lock calls around a symptom.

sections.title: Audit a lock from the data outward
sections.content:
Start with the data rather than the Mutex field. List every method and goroutine that can read or modify it. If some path bypasses the guard, locking the others does not repair the memory-ordering gap. Make the state unexported and channel access through methods that implement one rule.

Next trace lock balance. A successful Lock must reach exactly one Unlock. A defer is robust across multiple returns, but its scope still matters: deferring inside a long loop keeps every iteration's lock until the outer function returns. In that situation, move one iteration into a helper or unlock explicitly with carefully reviewed paths.

Then inspect identity. A value receiver copies its receiver, including an embedded Mutex. Returning a used synchronization-bearing struct by value has the same problem. Pointer receivers communicate that calls share one object. `go vet`'s copylocks analyzer catches common cases, but design should make copying unnatural even without a warning.

Finally, draw waits. If A holds lock one and requests lock two while B holds lock two and requests lock one, neither can proceed. Establish one global acquisition order or replace the pair with one lock around the joint invariant. Also mark channel sends, receives, callbacks, and I/O performed while locked because they can hide another wait edge.

The safe cache example returns a fresh map from Snapshot. Returning the internal map would let callers mutate it after Unlock and bypass every method. Encapsulation therefore extends beyond the Lock calls: references to protected mutable state must not escape unless their ownership and synchronization contract remains explicit.

sections.title: Mistake, symptom, and repair
sections.content:
| Mistake | Symptom | Repair |
|---|---|---|
| Copy used Mutex | Different guards for related state | Share one pointer |
| Miss Unlock | Permanent waiter | Defer or prove every exit |
| Lock only writes | Race report | Guard conflicting reads too |
| Lock twice | Self-deadlock | Non-recursive call structure |
| Reverse lock order | Cyclic deadlock | One global order or one lock |
